f-P21f: I also looked through the research corpus for good documentation of an actual case, a child in an intentional community who remained seriously dangerous to other people, with the whole sequence on record: the conduct, the assessment, the intervention, the review, and what happened later. I couldn't find any. It's possible that records are private, or that cases were referred elsewhere. Whatever the reason, I can't claim communities already know how to handle the hardest cases on their own. In those cases, the child, the family, and the people at risk all need access to competent help and review, outside the control of the home community.
f-P25b3: Kids also need transferable skills and education, relationships with people outside the community, access to their own records and documents, and at least one plausible next step (school, an apprenticeship, work, family, or another community). It would be great if the community could also provide resources to smooth the transition, like temporary housing, travel expenses, tools or a little money, but even if it can't, it can at least not make things worse by punishing people for leaving, or by holding back knowledge or records a young adult would need to function outside the community. No upbringing can provide perfect freedom, and the point isn't to erase path dependence. It's to not turn belonging into a trap.
